Swiss rail lines warped 97 times during heat wave as expert warns of derailment risk
Switzerland's rail network faced repeated track deformations during a summer heat wave, with 97 cases of warping or compression highlighting the pressure extreme temperatures can put on rail infrastructure.
Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) said the incidents did not compromise safety, though an expert cautioned that heat-stressed rails can increase derailment risk.
Here's what to know
Compared with the prior year, heat-related track problems climbed sharply on the SBB network in summer 2026. SBB logged 97 cases of track warping and compression deformation, according to Swissinfo. Swissinfo, citing SonntagsZeitung, said that was nearly four times the previous year's total.
While SBB said the added deformations and settlement did not affect rail safety, Patrick Braess, a specialist at ETH Zurich, said high temperatures can increase derailment risk.
The issue comes down to how steel behaves in high temperatures. As heat rises, rails expand, and if the track structure cannot absorb that stress, it can warp or deform under compression.
The 2026 cases point to a broader challenge for transportation systems during increasingly hot summers. Rail networks depend on precision, and even small changes in track geometry can force operators to increase inspections and maintenance.
More background
When extreme heat damages rail lines, it can disrupt commutes, freight movement, and emergency transportation while increasing risks for passengers, rail workers, and nearby communities, making it both a public safety and economic concern.
If trains must slow down, undergo additional maintenance, or temporarily alter service, workers may struggle to get to work, businesses may face shipping delays, and public agencies may face higher repair costs. Heat waves also carry direct health risks, especially for older adults, outdoor workers, and others exposed to prolonged high temperatures.
SBB's 2026 experience shows how one heat wave can repeatedly strain a rail network rather than cause a single, isolated defect in one location. The company said it routinely checks tracks with measurement and diagnostic vehicles.
The company described the heat as exceptional and, in response, created a dedicated working group after the summer of 2026.
What's being done?
SBB said it is pursuing targeted solutions rather than relying on a single quick fix. One key step is using concrete sleepers, which SBB said remain more stable than wooden ones under extreme heat stress.
Swissinfo reported that the railway is raising the welding neutralization temperature to help rails cope with higher baseline heat. The goal is to help the track structure handle expansion during hotter weather without deforming as easily.
SBB has also experimented with painting tracks white to cool them. The company said the treatment initially reduced temperatures by about 8.1 degrees Fahrenheit (4.5 degrees Celsius) on average, but after two years the benefit fell by roughly half because of soiling. Heavier traffic also wears down the effect faster.
Even with that reduced effectiveness, SBB has not ruled out the method. The company said it is still studying whether white coatings may make sense in specific situations, while its working group continues assessing where additional measures are needed.

The World Health Organization (WHO), the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), UNICEF and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) Wednesday has launched the first-ever set of priority indicators to help countries track the health impacts of heat on pregnant women, newborns and children.
The new framework comes amid rising global temperatures and growing evidence that heat exposure poses serious health risks, particularly for vulnerable populations.
- Advertisement -
It is designed to strengthen preparedness, improve monitoring, accelerate response and help in protection of some of the populations most vulnerable to climate-related health risks.
In a statement, WHO says studies show that exposure to extreme heat can harm health from pregnancy to childhood, leading to a 26% increase in the odds of preterm birth.
Similarly, newborns are increasingly exposed, with babies under one year of age experiencing 389% more heatwave days in 2024 compared with the 1986 to 2005 baseline period.
Globally, an estimated 1.5 billion children are exposed to heatwaves that are becoming more frequent, longer or more severe.
“As our world continues to heat up, it creates new risks for health, and older people, pregnant women, newborns and children are among those least able to escape them,” said Bruce Gordon, Director a.i. of WHO’s Department of Environment, Climate Change, One Health and Migration. “Our health systems need the data to recognize this reality and take action – from protecting people during heatwaves to embedding climate risk consideration into everyday health services.”
The new report recommends that countries monitor preterm births, stillbirths, low birthweight, pregnancy hypertension, child deaths and health-facility visits during extreme heat.
Monitoring school attendance can also help reveal how heat is disrupting children’s lives.
Dr Pascale Allotey, Director of WHO’s Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing, said tracking health outcomes alongside heat exposure would help countries identify potential impacts and protect vulnerable populations.
Routine health records, combined with temperature and other heat-exposure data, can help authorities detect unusual changes in health outcomes during extreme heat events, prompting further investigation and timely intervention.
“Heat is already affecting our most vulnerable populations, including pregnant women, newborns and children. But what health systems do not count, they cannot respond to,” said Dr Pascale Allotey, Director of WHO’s Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing.
“By tracking outcomes such as preterm birth, child deaths and illnesses, and health-facility visits alongside heat exposure, countries can identify potential impacts and take action to protect women and children,” he added.
Routine health data and heat-exposure data such as air temperature can help identify possible heat-related signals that can assist countries in identifying unusual changes during periods of extreme, conduct further investigation and act accordingly.
The information can help health authorities prepare facilities for increased demand, strengthen warnings to pregnant women and families, identify communities at greatest risk and improve heat-health planning.
As extreme heat is fast becoming a common feature of a warming world, WHO is calling on countries to strengthen their ability to monitor and respond to its health impacts.
By using the new priority indicators in this report, governments can better identify risks, target interventions and protect pregnant women, newborns and children from preventable harm.
Further, WHO urges all countries to develop and implement heat-health action plans that are context-specific, and that integrate the needs of these vulnerable populations, strengthen early warning systems and trigger timely action when heat risks emerge.

Hobart hits 31.7 degrees as heatwave warning stays for east coast
Pulse Tasmania
Hobart reached 31.7 degrees this afternoon, as several weather stations across Tasmania recorded some of their warmest October days in recent years.
Bureau of Meteorology data shows the city’s temperature peaked at 3:19pm and was still 28.1 degrees at 6:50pm.

Campania also reached 31.7 degrees. Dunalley recorded 31.4 degrees, Hobart Airport 31.2 and Bushy Park 31.1.
On the West Coast, Strahan reached 30.7 degrees just after midday.
The bureau’s records show Launceston Airport had its warmest October day in 22 years of records, with the temperature climbing to 28 degrees.
Strahan and Dunalley both recorded their third-warmest October day, Strahan in 38 years of records and Dunalley in 14 years. Launceston had its fourth-warmest October day in 46 years.
Winds were also strong, with gusts reaching 61km/h in Hobart and 80km/h on kunanyi/Mount Wellington.
The bureau has issued a severe heatwave warning for the east coast, with St Helens among the locations likely to be affected.

It has cancelled the warning for the south-east, saying severe heatwave conditions there have dropped below warning thresholds.
The bureau said maximum temperatures in the high 20s to around 30 degrees would peak on Thursday and Friday.
Overnight minimums are expected in the low to mid teens before conditions ease more broadly over the weekend.
Hobart is forecast to reach 30 degrees on Friday, with an 80% chance of showers, most likely in the afternoon and evening.

full_text:
Debris being cleared from the railway tracks after a landslip near the Parassala Railway Station in Thiruvananthapuram on Thursday (October 22, 2026).

The northeast monsoon has entered a vigorous phase over Keralam, triggering widespread rainfall, particularly along the Western Ghats, under the influence of weather systems over the Bay of Bengal. Several areas received intense rain accompanied by lightning and gusty winds, resulting in waterlogging and minor landslips.
Overnight rain on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) triggered landslips along the railway line between Thiruvananthapuram and Nagercoil, derailing the locomotive of Bilaspur-Tirunelveli Superfast Express near Parassala in the early hours of Thursday. The locomotive derailed between Neyyattinkara and Parassala, near the Parassala railway station, around 2.19 a.m. No injuries have been reported.
Rail traffic disrupted
The incident disrupted rail traffic along the southern Keralam-Nagercoil-Kanyakumari region, forcing the railway authorities to detain, cancel or reschedule more than a dozen trains. Services were restored around 9.30 a.m. after restoration work, including re-railing and removing of the locomotive. After safety inspections, the Parasuram Express bound for Mangaluru left Parassala and safely crossed the affected section, after which train services were fully restored. A relief locomotive took the coaches of the derailed train back to Neyyattinkara, from where passengers were transported to various destinations by road.
Heavy rain
Meanwhile, the southern and central parts of Keralam received heavy rain with Mavelikara in Alappuzha and Venkurinji in Pathanamthitta recording the highest rainfall of 14 cm each in the 24 hours ending at 8.30 a.m. on Thursday (October 22, 2026), followed by Kayamkulam and Thycattussery in Alappuzha with 11 cm each.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast heavy rain across Keralam for the next four days under the influence of a low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal. The low-pressure area and its associated cyclonic circulation over the southwest Bay of Bengal and adjoining Tamil Nadu coast are feeding moisture into the State, resulting in heavy to very heavy rain, particularly over the Ghat regions and southern and central districts.
Another low-pressure area is likely to form over the southeast and adjoining east-central Bay of Bengal around October 23, 2026. As the system moves northwestwards and intensifies, it is likely to trigger heavy rainfall in Keralam with the system enhancing moisture flow towards peninsular India, potentially increasing rainfall over the State from October 23 to 26. Fairly widespread rain, accompanied by thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds, is expected during the period.
Orange alert
Malappuram, Kozhikode, Wayanad and Kannur were placed under an orange alert by the IMD on Thursday (October 22, 2026), with the possibility of intense thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds, while the remaining districts were under yellow alert for isolated heavy rain. For Friday (October 23, 2026), nine districts were placed under orange alert, while Malappuram, Palakkad, Thrissur, Ernakulam and Alappuzha were put on yellow alert. Heavy rain has also been forecast across Keralam on Saturday (October 24, 2026) and Sunday (October 25, 2026).

Heavy thunderstorms continued to lash several parts of Keralam on Thursday under the influence of a low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued an orange alert for four districts, warning of intense thunderstorms, while the remaining districts were placed under a yellow alert for heavy rain over the next 24 hours.
The eastern ghat regions, southern Keralam and parts of Central Travancore received heavy overnight rain on Wednesday, disrupting normal life and causing waterlogging in several areas. Disaster management authorities have been placed on high alert in view of the forecast for continued heavy rain.
Further, minor landslips triggered by the heavy rain along the Thiruvananthapuram-Nagercoil railway section near Parassala railway station in Keralam also disrupted train services. Several trains were detained or rescheduled, with services expected to resume along the affected route by 10 a.m.
According to the IMD, the low-pressure area and its associated cyclonic circulation over the southwest Bay of Bengal and adjoining Tamil Nadu coast are feeding moisture into Keralam, resulting in heavy to very heavy thunderstorms, particularly over the ghat regions and the southern and central parts of the State.
Another low-pressure area is likely to develop over the southeast and adjoining east-central Bay of Bengal around October 23. As the system moves northwestwards and intensifies, it could enhance the moisture flow towards peninsular India, leading to a gradual increase in rainfall over Keralam from October 23 to 25. The State is likely to receive fairly widespread rainfall during this period, with thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and gusty winds in several areas.
Ernakulam, Thrissur, Malappuram and Kozhikode are under an orange alert for Thursday, with the possibility of intense thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds over the next 24 hours.

title: Heavy rain likely in Tamil Nadu for 2 more days: Schools shut in Tirunelveli, Thoothukudi, Kanniyakumari and Tenkasi; Chennai on yellow alert | India News - Hindustan Times

full_text:
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) on Wednesday forecast more rainfall over Tamil Nadu for the next two days as a low-pressure area formed over the southwest Bay of Bengal, shutting down schools in several parts of the state.
Schools will remain closed on October 22 in Tirunelveli, Thoothukudi, Kanniyakumari and Tenkasi districts due to heavy rainfall. However, no school closure order has been issued for Chennai so far. All government and government-aided schools and private schools in Puducherry and Karaikal have been also declared a holiday on Thursday.
Heavy to very heavy rainfall that began on Tuesday continued overnight, with Chennai’s MGR Nagar recording the highest rainfall at 15 cm. Several neighbourhoods in and around the state capital received between 10 cm and 15 cm of rain. The IMD has issued a yellow alert for Chennai amid the heavy showers.
On October 22, heavy to very heavy rainfall is likely at isolated places, accompanied by thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds reaching speeds of 40-50 kmph at one or two locations, the IMD predicted, according to PTI news agency.
The districts likely to experience such rainfall include Thoothukudi, Tirunelveli, Kanyakumari, Tenkasi, Virudhunagar, Ramanathapuram, Theni, Dindigul, Madurai, Coimbatore, the Nilgiris, Sivaganga, Pudukkottai, Thanjavur, Tiruvarur, Nagapattinam and Mayiladuthurai, along with Karaikal in Puducherry.
On October 23, widespread rainfall is expected to continue. “Heavy to very heavy rain at isolated places with thunderstorm & lightning with gusty wind speed reaching 40-50 kmph at one or two places is likely to occur over Kanyakumari, Nilgiris and Coimbatore,” an IMD bulletin said.
Meanwhile, schools were closed on October 21 in Chennai, Tiruvallur, Kancheepuram and Chengalpattu districts due to heavy rainfall. However, no orders directing school closures in these districts on October 22 had been issued so far.
